- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.5) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.3), model often underestimates; adjust upward by 1–2% to reflect bearish sentiment’s reversal bias.
- Model frequently overshoots after sharp price spikes (e.g., +5–10% from recent peak); cap forecast at 10–15% above recent high.
- If 3–5 consecutive days show mean reversion (price moving back toward 70–72 range), model tends to lag; shift forecast 1–2 days ahead to align with momentum.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.3–0.7), model overfits short-term noise; smooth forecast by averaging last 5–7 days’ trend.
- When sentiment is high and price is rising, model often fails to capture “sustained breakout” — increase forecast slope slightly to reflect sentiment momentum.
- If sentiment is low and price is falling, model underestimates “bottoming” — add 1–3% to forecast to account for sentiment-driven rebound.
